guides.title: Flood Preparedness & Survival
guides.description: Critical actions before flood waters rise and while escaping inundated areas.
steps: Monitor local broadcasts or dial 1090 for flood advisory and warnings.
Store drinking water in sealed containers and move dry food, medicines, and documents to higher ground.
Turn off electricity main switches and gas supplies before water enters your house.
If instructed to evacuate, do so immediately using identified safe elevated routes.
Never walk, swim, or drive through flowing water — 6 inches of fast water can knock you down.
thingsToDo: Move livestock, valuables, and family members to elevated ground or flood shelters.
Drink only boiled, purified, or chlorine-treated water.
Keep a long wooden pole to test ground firmness when walking through shallow water.
thingsToAvoid: Do not allow children to play in or near floodwaters.
Do not drive or walk through flooded bridges or submerged culverts.
Do not touch electrical switches or appliances while standing in wet areas.

guides.title: Cyclone & Coastal Storm Shelter
guides.description: Actions during cyclone alert signals and seeking designated shelter.
steps: Listen to regular radio / TV alerts and understand maritime cyclone warning signals.
Secure loose roof sheets, cut weak tree branches close to dwelling structures.
Pack an emergency bag with dry food, water, flashlight, battery radio, and first aid.
Evacuate to the nearest designated cyclone shelter before gale force winds arrive.
Remain inside the shelter until authorities officially declare the storm has fully passed.
thingsToDo: Head to the nearest concrete cyclone shelter well before wind intensifies.
Help elderly individuals, pregnant women, and children reach safe shelters early.
Unplug all electrical equipment and turn off gas cylinders.
thingsToAvoid: Do not venture outdoors when the eye of the storm arrives — winds will suddenly reverse violently.
Do not spread rumors or disregard evacuation orders.
Do not seek shelter under unanchored tin roofs or near power poles.

guides.title: If a Fire Starts at Home
guides.description: How to get out quickly and safely when there is a fire in your home.
steps: Alert everyone in the home and get out immediately. Do not stop to collect belongings.
Stay low and crawl under smoke toward the exit.
Feel doors with the back of your hand before opening. If hot, use an alternate escape route.
Close doors behind you to slow down the fire and smoke spread.
Go outside to an agreed assembly point and call emergency services (999 or 16163) immediately.
thingsToDo: Get out first, then call for help.
Crawl low under smoke.
If clothes catch fire: Stop, Drop and Roll to extinguish flames.
thingsToAvoid: Do not go back inside for any reason.
Do not open a hot door.
Do not use elevators during a fire.

guides.title: Drop, Cover, and Hold On
guides.description: What to do during tremors and when the shaking stops.
steps: DROP down onto your hands and knees immediately.
COVER your head and neck under a sturdy table or desk.
HOLD ON to your shelter until shaking stops. Be prepared for it to move.
If no shelter is nearby, drop next to an interior wall and protect your head with your arms.
When shaking stops, check for gas leaks, fires, and structural damage before exiting cautiously.
thingsToDo: Stay where you are until shaking stops completely.
Take stairs, never elevators, when exiting damaged structures.
Expect aftershocks and be ready to Drop, Cover, and Hold On again.
thingsToAvoid: Do not run outside during shaking — falling masonry and glass cause the most injuries.
Do not stand in doorways (modern doorways are not stronger than walls).
Do not use matches or lighters until you are sure gas lines are intact.

guides.title: Lightning & Thunderstorm Safety
guides.description: Surviving severe lightning strikes in open areas and indoors.
steps: When thunder roars, go indoors. Seek shelter inside a substantial building or hard-topped vehicle.
If caught in an open field, crouch down in a ball-like position with your hands over your ears and feet close together.
Stay away from tall isolated trees, wire fences, power lines, and open water bodies.
Avoid using corded electrical appliances or taking showers during a heavy thunderstorm.
Wait at least 30 minutes after hearing the last thunderclap before leaving your shelter.
thingsToDo: Get off open fields, rooftops, and ponds as soon as dark storm clouds gather.
Crouch low on the balls of your feet to minimize ground contact if stranded in the open.
Immediately provide CPR if someone is struck — lightning victims carry no electrical charge.
thingsToAvoid: Do not shelter under solitary tall trees.
Do not hold metal farm tools, umbrellas with metal tips, or touch wire fences.
Do not lie flat on the ground (ground current travels easily across a prone body).

guides.title: Road Accident Scene Safety
guides.description: Protecting victims and avoiding secondary collisions at a crash scene.
steps: Stop safely, switch on hazard lights, and place reflective warning markers 50m behind the scene.
Turn off the ignition of involved vehicles to minimize fuel fire danger.
Call 999 immediately with your location, number of injured persons, and severity.
Do not move unconscious or trapped victims unless there is immediate threat of fire or explosion.
Administer basic bleeding control with firm, clean pressure while waiting for rescue teams.
thingsToDo: Keep yourself and other helpers visible and away from moving oncoming traffic.
Support the injured person's head and neck to prevent spinal injury.
Reassure conscious casualties and keep them calm and warm.
thingsToAvoid: Do not remove a motorcycle rider's helmet unless their airway is blocked.
Do not give food or drink to injured persons who may need surgery.
Do not smoke or use open flames near crash vehicles.

guides.title: Severe Bleeding & Shock
guides.description: Immediate direct pressure technique to control heavy blood loss.
steps: Apply firm, continuous direct pressure to the wound with a clean cloth or sterile dressing.
Maintain heavy pressure for at least 5 to 10 minutes without lifting the pad to peek.
If blood soaks through, add another pad on top — do not remove the original dressing.
Lay the person flat and keep them warm with a blanket to prevent circulatory shock.
Call 999 or transport to the nearest medical emergency department immediately.
thingsToDo: Press hard and continuously directly on the wound site.
Wear disposable gloves or use a plastic barrier if available.
Keep the casualty resting quietly to maintain steady blood pressure.
thingsToAvoid: Do not remove objects deeply embedded in a wound — bandage around them.
Do not clean a severe, spurting wound yourself — control bleeding first.
Do not apply a makeshift tourniquet unless you have formal training.
guides.sourceName: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent

tips.text: Turn Around, Don't Drown! Never walk, swim or drive through moving flood waters.
Keep copies of national ID and deeds in waterproof zip bags stored in an accessible high place.
When cyclone warning signal 8 or higher is raised, move promptly to your assigned shelter.
Keep an emergency bag ready with dry biscuits, flashlight, battery radio, and matches.
If caught in smoke, crawl on your hands and knees where cleaner cooler air is close to the floor.
When ground shakes: Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Avoid running out into falling glass or bricks.
When thunder roars, go indoors. Stay away from isolated tall trees and open water bodies.
At a crash scene, make the area safe first with hazard lights before approaching casualties.
For severe bleeding, continuous direct pressure with a clean cloth is the primary life-saver.
